Waterside Plaza, a residential complex in NYC’s Kips Bay along the East River, was envisioned in 1961 by developer Richard Ravitch to address housing shortages for UN staff. Built on a platform over the river—supported by 2,000 steel piles sunk 80 feet into the riverbed—it opened in 1973, with completion in 1974. Designed by Davis, Brody & Associates, it features four brown-brick towers (31 to 37 stories) and duplex townhouses around a two-acre plaza, originally part of the Mitchell-Lama affordable housing program. The site, east of the FDR Drive, used landfill from England and was isolated, accessible only by a pedestrian overpass at 25th Street. It won a Construction Achievement Award in 1974 from the American Society of Civil Engineers. Plans for further waterfront expansion in the 1980s were scrapped, and Stuyvesant Cove Park took its place. Once home to a diverse mix of income groups, it’s now a luxury rental community managed by Brookfield Properties, known for its river views and self-contained feel.

name: Grove Court
description: A hidden courtyard of six townhouses located in Greenwich Village, Manhattan.
history: Grove Court was developed in the 1850s by Samuel Cocks, a local grocer, to provide housing for working-class families. The courtyard's secluded nature made it a quiet retreat within the bustling city. Over time, it has become a charming and sought-after residential enclave.
note:
The story of Grove Court begins in the mid-19th century. In 1848, Samuel Cocks, a grocer with a store at the corner of Grove and Bedford Streets, acquired the rear yards of properties along Grove Street from Samuel Stryker, who had been leasing the land from Trinity Church. Cocks saw an opportunity to create housing for working-class families, likely with the practical aim of securing a steady customer base for his grocery business. Construction of the six three-story Federal-style houses began shortly after and was completed in 1854. Initially, these homes were considered a single tax lot, addressed as 10½ Grove Street, and were modest in size—about 990 square feet each—compared to the larger townhouses typical of the era.

In its early days, Grove Court was far from the picturesque retreat it is today. Built for laborers and tradesmen, the enclave was a working-class community, and its secluded location behind the main street contributed to its reputation as a less desirable area. Historical accounts suggest it was once a rough spot, even earning the nickname "Mixed Ale Alley" due to the drinking habits of its residents. Photographs from the early 20th century, such as those by Jessie Tarbox Beals and Arthur D. Chapman, show laundry hanging in the courtyard, a testament to its utilitarian roots.

name: Patchin Place
description: A small, gated alley in Greenwich Village, lined with historic townhouses.
history: Patchin Place was developed in the 1840s and has been home to various artists and writers, including E.E. Cummings and Djuna Barnes. The alley's quaint atmosphere and historic architecture make it a unique part of the Village's cultural landscape.
note: Patchin Place, a tiny gated cul-de-sac off West 10th Street in Greenwich Village, New York City, was developed in 1848–1849 by Aaron Patchin, a surveyor who built ten three-story brick row houses on land he acquired from his father-in-law, Samuel Milligan. Originally designed as modest housing—possibly for workers at the nearby Brevoort House hotel—the homes featured small dormer windows and shared a courtyard with a gas lamp, still lit today. Early residents were largely working-class, including Basque immigrants who ran boarding houses there in the late 19th century. By the early 20th century, Patchin Place transformed into a bohemian enclave, attracting literary and artistic figures like E.E. Cummings, who lived at No. 4 from 1923 until his death in 1962, and Djuna Barnes, a resident of No. 5 for over 40 years. Theodore Dreiser and John Reed also spent time there, cementing its reputation as a creative haven. Rumors persist that the houses were built with salvaged bricks from the 1832 demolition of Newgate Prison, though this lacks firm evidence. Part of the Greenwich Village Historic District since 1969, Patchin Place remains a quiet, historic retreat, its charm preserved amid the bustling city.

name: Milligan Place
description: A tiny, triangular courtyard in Greenwich Village, featuring four townhouses.
history: Milligan Place was created in the 1850s and named after its developer, Samuel Milligan. Like Patchin Place, it has a rich history of housing artists and writers, contributing to the Village's reputation as a bohemian enclave.
note: Milligan Place, a secluded triangular courtyard in Greenwich Village, New York City, was constructed in 1852 by Aaron Patchin, who named it after his father-in-law, Daniel Milligan. Originally built as boarding houses for waiters from the nearby Brevoort House hotel, the four three-story brick homes were modest and housed working-class residents. Located off Sixth Avenue between West 10th and 11th Streets, it was once a gritty, overlooked spot, dubbed a "hole in the wall" by a 1915 New York Times article. In the early 20th century, it gained cultural significance as home to notable figures like playwright Eugene O’Neill and Provincetown Players founders George Cram Cook and Susan Glaspell. Over time, the courtyard transformed from a rough enclave to a charming, gated retreat, reflecting Greenwich Village’s shift from working-class roots to artistic haven. Designated part of the Greenwich Village Historic District in 1969, Milligan Place now commands high rents and epitomizes the area’s historic allure.

name: Pomander Walk
description: A Tudor-style residential complex located on the Upper West Side of Manhattan.
history: Pomander Walk was built in the 1920s and designed to resemble a quaint English village. The complex includes 27 buildings with half-timbered facades and is a designated New York City landmark, celebrated for its distinctive architecture.
note:
Inspired by a 1910 romantic comedy play by Louis N. Parker called Pomander Walk—set in a fictional London lane—Healy intended it as a temporary project to generate income while he raised funds for a grand hotel. Designed by the New York architecture firm King and Campbell, the two- and three-story homes feature stucco, brick, and half-timber facades, evoking an English village. Healy’s death in 1927 halted his hotel plans, leaving Pomander Walk as a permanent fixture.

Originally an all-rental complex with about 61 units (each building typically had one apartment per floor), it housed theatrical folks like Rosalind Russell and Humphrey Bogart, drawn to its whimsy. By the 1970s, it had deteriorated and faced demolition, but residents fought back, securing its designation as a New York City Landmark and a spot on the National Register of Historic Places in 1982. A 2009 renovation restored its pastel charm—think green, blue, and red facades with flower boxes—earning it a preservation award.

name: Sylvan Terrace
description: A cobblestone street in Washington Heights, lined with wooden row houses.
history: Sylvan Terrace was built in the 1880s as part of the Morris-Jumel Mansion estate. The houses were originally intended for working-class families but have since been restored and are now part of a historic district, reflecting the area's 19th-century charm.
note: Sylvan Terrace, a charming cobblestone street in Upper Manhattan’s Washington Heights, was developed in 1882 by William Paulding Jr. as part of the Morris-Jumel estate, originally the site of James Jumel’s 1765 mansion. Designed by architect Gilbert Rantus Bishop, this single-block enclave between West 160th and 161st Streets features 20 identical two-story wooden row houses with brick foundations, built in a simplified Queen Anne style. Intended as affordable housing for working-class tenants like maids and coachmen, the homes replaced earlier farm structures after Paulding subdivided the land following Jumel’s death. The name “Sylvan” nods to the wooded, rural feel of the area at the time, though it’s now a rare surviving frame-house street in Manhattan. By the early 20th century, the terrace fell into disrepair, but its proximity to the Morris-Jumel Mansion—George Washington’s 1776 headquarters—helped it gain recognition. Designated a New York City Landmark in 1975 and part of the Jumel Terrace Historic District, it was restored in the late 1970s by the Landmarks Preservation Commission and local owners. Today, these gaslit homes, painted in pastel shades, are prized residential properties, with sales—like No. 14 in 2023 for $1.1 million—reflecting their historic allure and scarcity.
